description_full: Climb Global Solutions, Inc. operates as a value-added information technology (IT) distribution and solutions company in the United States, Canada, Europe, and the United Kingdom. The company operates through two segments, Distribution and Solutions. It distributes technical software to corporate and value-added resellers, consultants, and systems integrators under the name Climb Channel Solutions; and provides cloud solutions and resells software, hardware, and services under the name Grey Matter. The company also resells computer software and hardware developed by others, as well as provides technical services to end user customers. In addition, it offers a line of products from various software vendors; and tools for virtualization/cloud computing, security, networking, storage and infrastructure management, application lifecycle management, and other technically sophisticated domains, as well as computer hardware. The company markets its products through its own web sites, local seminars, events, webinars, and social media, as well as direct email and printed materials. In addition, the company offers wholesale (intercompany trade) of computers, computer peripheral equipment and software, as well as distributes cybersecurity, cloud services and virtualization services across the French market. Climb Global Solutions, Inc. was formerly known as Wayside Technology Group, Inc. and changed its name to Climb Global Solutions, Inc. in October 2022. Climb Global Solutions, Inc. was incorporated in 1982 and is headquartered in Eatontown, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Climb Global Solutions, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $741M market cap on $653M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +29% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 40% against a 9% cost of capital — a 31-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $15M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.78× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.7%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 12% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
